newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian parliament set to blast Yeltsin reshuffle.
newsitem.headline: Russian parliament set to blast Yeltsin reshuffle.

text.p: Russian communist deputies on Wednesday blasted plans by President Boris Yeltsin for a far-reaching cabinet reshuffle designed to give liberal reformers a free hand with the economy.
In a toughly worded draft resolution due to be debated later in the day by the State Duma lower house of parliament, they said the reshuffle would lead Russia to economic ruin.

"The changes carried out in the government again illustrate the desire of the current authorities to continue the ruinous social-economic course which has brought Russia to the brink of catastrophe," said the draft motion.
The communists, the biggest faction in the Duma, have been enraged by Yeltsin's decision to make his liberal ally Anatoly Chubais sole First Deputy Prime Minister.

The resolution called his appointment a "direct challenge to social opinion in Russia, a factor in the subsequent worsening of relations between the presidential and executive authorities and the federal assembly".

Chubais, applauded in the West as an uncompromising liberal reformer, is hated by the communists for masterminding Yeltsin's successful re-election campaign last year and for his role in overseeing privatisation, in which they say state assets were sold off cheaply.

Yeltsin on Tuesday ordered Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin to present proposals for the government changes within a week, making clear that only the premier and Chubais were sure of keeping their jobs.
Yeltsin's decree did not say the government had to submit a formal resignation and the Duma has no legal right to prevent him forming a new cabinet because the premier remains in place.
But the communists have already threatened a no-confidence motion in the government. If voted through twice, it would pose Yeltsin with the choice of dismissing the cabinet or the Duma itself.
Given Russia's deep-seated economic and social problems, which include serious wage and pension arrears, a fresh election might return an even less cooperative Duma.
